brief.welcome: Welcome. You have joined SchemaForge, and the person who brought you here is about to work with you on it. This brief gives you, in order, the mission, the architecture, what is needed now and how to start; then the method, everything to read, and the rules. Take it in whole, tell your human what you understood, and the two of you can start.
brief.intro: You were pointed here to understand SchemaForge or to help someone contribute to it. Read this brief whole, then the files it lists in the order given, then report back to your human before you change anything. Everything here is read from the repository (https://github.com/k8nstantin/schema-forge, branch main); the files are the authority, this brief only orders them.
brief.if-task-file: Stop reading this brief. A task file (specs/tasks/*.xml) is a complete instruction: follow its start element exactly. You may be in any session: build from the files alone, read whole in the method's order, and take nothing said earlier as authority. Nothing here adds to or overrides it.

mission.product: An open-source, intelligent, multi-engine schema design and management tool, where a coding agent and an architect work on the same live design through MCP, and nothing lands unchecked: a schema designed from scratch, reverse-engineered from a database, converted from one engine to another, its intelligence stored with it. Every database is an engine plugin, and the engines come in families: two full-feature engines, engine_mysql and engine_postgresql, each built once across every version of its database, and every managed service, distribution or compatible database falls into its family as a subset of it (MySQL: Percona Server, Amazon RDS, Cloud SQL, Amazon Aurora, TiDB; PostgreSQL: Amazon RDS, Cloud SQL, Amazon Aurora, AlloyDB, Spanner, CockroachDB), declared as facts and checked, not built again: what looks like a dozen engines is two, by the design of the schema. At the centre stands the database SchemaForge keeps its work in: one PostgreSQL database, schema_forge, in the PostgreSQL 18 bundled with the app, every design rows of it under its UUIDv7, holding the cortex every engine shares and each engine's own tables, each owner in its own namespace, designed before any of it is built and locked so every build falls into it.
mission.purpose: SchemaForge builds two things together: the product, and the method it is built by, in which people and coding agents develop together: a design session fixes the database and writes a task file; one agent builds it in one session; gates and a person's review decide; a build's lesson changes the method. Every contributor works the same way, with their own coding agent, and the method is theirs to improve too. And it is a collaborative learning exercise, in the open: people learn a data product from the inside (database design, engines, conversion, CDC, a schema's intelligence), coding with agents, and spec-driven development, by building one together.

architecture.note: How SchemaForge is put together, each part with the file that decides it. Read those files before you rely on any of this.
architecture.part: The process (the canvas, the MCP, turns and undo, the rules, the store) is shared by every database and names none of them. Everything about one database (its types, kinds, options, how it is read and written, its own tables) belongs to its engine: one plugin, with its own namespace, owner and service account, plugged into the cortex in five checked steps.

Two full-feature engines are built, each once across every version of its database: engine_mysql and engine_postgresql. Every managed service, distribution and compatible database is a subset that falls into its family as a flavor: MySQL's Percona Server, RDS, Cloud SQL, Aurora and TiDB; PostgreSQL's RDS, Cloud SQL, Aurora, AlloyDB, Spanner and CockroachDB. What a flavor refuses is a declared fact; what it adds is a typed table for a new kind, a flavor_options key for a new option. What looks like a dozen engines is two (decision service-plugins).

SchemaForge keeps its work in a PostgreSQL 18 with pgvector it bundles: one database, schema_forge, and every design in it is rows under its UUIDv7, never a database or a namespace of its own. Each owner's tables are in its own namespace (cortex, the workspace's among them, ui, engine_<id>, and a feature's own); every reference is a foreign key, every column documented in the database, and every rule a foreign key cannot state is enforced by the database at commit. Every change is an operation of a turn, logged, so it can be undone.

Every engine's first feature is a schema opened from a saved connection: the server's version first, then only what it has and only what the person chose (everything, or definitions, metadata and usage, by kind and object), read gently, with the server's own usage kept beside the design; every step shown on the read screen. MySQL first, from 5.7.

The cortex, the workspace, every engine and every feature is an owner: its own folder, card, namespace, rules, seeds and versions. A change adds; a rename takes two versions. A new engine or feature starts from the owner template.

crates/model, the schema skeleton every engine shares; crates/engine, the engine interface, the section layout, the registry and the conformance kit; crates/engines, the registry of the shipped engines (built by the sequence); crates/store, the store over the bundled PostgreSQL (built by the sequence); engines/<engine>, one crate per database, each with its schema folder engines/<engine>/schema; schema/cortex and schema/workspace, the cortex's and the workspace's tables; tools/architecture, the design checked on the code; tools/specs, the spec check (built by the sequence); tools/check.py, the one command every change passes; specs/, this spec; docs/, the design, as XML (the site renders each doc as a page for people).

specs/ holds the root (purpose, authority, method, sequence, decisions), the rules, this brief, the lessons and one task file per build. The spec is written before the code, and the code falls into it.

first-steps.note: You do not need to know all of it to make a useful first contribution: your agent reads the project with you. Mistakes are caught before they land, in three ways: the checks every pull request runs (format, lint, every test, the architecture check and the spec check), the lock on the database's design, and a person's review. Each step below is small, real, and teaches something; building a task or an engine takes real skill, and these steps build it.
first-steps.step: Ask in Discussions how something works or why it was decided. It is answered in the open, so the next person finds it, and what confused you shows us where the docs are thin.

step.name: tell us what your agent understood

first-steps.step: Point your agent at this brief, then post what it explained back to you and where it was wrong. The brief is how every agent learns the project; your report tests it, and the fix helps every agent after yours.

Engines are proved against real schemas, not toy ones. A dump or hand-written schema of a database you know (schema only: no data, no secrets) becomes a sample every build of that engine must read and write back exactly. You learn where SQL hides its corners.

step.name: fix a page or a doc

first-steps.step: If a sentence took you two reads, it will take the next person two reads. Rewrite it in a pull request: pages and docs change like code, through the checks and a review, so you learn the whole path a change takes.

A task file is a complete instruction: what to build, its steps, its tests and the checks that decide. Give it to your agent in a fresh session, review what it builds, then submit. This is where you learn the method end to end; others may build the same task, and the best build is merged.

start.step: Read this brief whole, then the files of its reading list, in order.

Brief your human, in your own words and in a few minutes of reading: what SchemaForge is and why (the mission), how it is put together (the architecture), and where it stands (what is built, what is next).

Tell them they can start where they are, with you reading the project alongside them and the checks catching mistakes before they land, and show them the roster: the small first steps, then every contribution open now, one line each, from this brief's wanted list: the tasks ready to build, the tasks queued, the guides (a new engine), the decisions waiting for a design session, and the good first issues. For each: what it is, what it would teach them, and what it takes.

Let them pick what interests them. Tell them that anyone may take up the same task, that every build is reviewed side by side, and that the best one is merged: a build that is not merged still teaches, and its lesson improves the method.

To build a task: on a fresh checkout of main, point an agent at the task file's path, in any session; it builds from the files alone, and the pull request is opened under your own GitHub account. For a new database: the engine guide, from its first phase. For an issue or anything new: open the conversation on GitHub first, with your human's word.

method.note: Every part of the product is built this way, by the maintainer and by every contributor, each with their own coding agent.
method.step: A person and an agent, with the maintainer, design or change the database in the owners' folders and write the work down as a task file under specs/tasks, every decision dated in specs/root.xml.

One agent, in any session, on a checkout of main, pointed at one task file and working from the files alone. It reads in the order the root gives, builds only what the file says, decides only what it lists, and stops when anything is missing or two files disagree, rather than guess.
Every gate of the task file runs (local, Docker, CI), and their results go into the pull request.
A person reviews and merges; the agent never merges.
What a build taught is added to specs/lessons.xml, and a design session changes the method or the rules because of it. The method is open to improvement like the code.

ways.way: Any task listed as wanted is open to everyone at once: your human points an agent, in any session, at the task file's path (specs/tasks/<file>.xml) on a fresh checkout of main; it builds from the files alone and opens the pull request under your human's GitHub account. Others may build the same task; the maintainer reviews the builds side by side and merges the best. It may be you, once you have read the files whole and set aside this conversation as authority.

An engine, a feature, a fix: for a new database, follow specs/guides/engine.xml from its first phase; otherwise your human opens an issue or a discussion; the design is agreed in a design session and written as a task file; then it is built as above.
A lesson, a rule that would have caught a mistake, a clearer step: proposed in Discussions, decided in a design session.

brief.database: Every table is a file of an owner's folder, one CREATE TABLE each, every column commented, its comments also in the database. Read a folder's files to know its tables; the owner template explains the shapes.

open.decision: The operation kinds (add_table, rename_column and the rest), what each changes and how the agent calls it.
Whether an agent's change enters the current model as it is made, the turn open until a verdict, or is staged until accepted.

The tables of the rules: their links on the hierarchy, groups, exceptions, packs and findings (docs/rules.xml), as their own owner and namespace in schema_forge; the integrity rules on ice in lab/on-ice/rules return with them, each checking only the designs a commit changed.
The tables of a CDC pipeline between two schemas, by their stable ids.

What is worked out about the model, kept apart from it in a feature owner insight, so a person or an agent can search and question a design through the MCP: the links between objects, derived from their bodies, never typed: one row per fact a body states about another object (calls, reads, writes, on, references, creates, drops, alters, foreign key, or unresolved), with the object it names when it resolves, the line and the statement it was read from as evidence, and for a name built while it runs the pattern of its fixed parts, so one fact can name every table it can reach; walked both ways for impact (2.0, decision definitions-first); cards composed mechanically from the model; annotations an agent writes, with the model and the input hash; embeddings (pgvector, HNSW) of cards and annotations, searched together with full-text and exact names and every hit confirmed against the model. Kept fresh from the log: an accepted turn's row_changes name the objects whose rows are redone. Rebuilt, never logged or migrated. The MCP's read tools: search (finds candidates), object (one object whole), impact (the walk), sql (every count and list, as a read-only role). The embedding model is the decision embedding-models. A semantic layer (business terms, measures) is authored, so it is its own owner, logged by turns; its embeddings are insight's.

What the steward agent may do alone and what stays a person's: which pull requests it may merge (a task's build, a contributor's, a design session's never), what its review must prove beyond the gates, how often it runs and on what, how it records a lesson, how it starts the next build, and how a person stops or overrides it. Until it closes, a person reviews and merges, and no agent merges.
The order of the work after the store: which of the insight layer, the rules, the MCP's tools, the operations and the canvas come first, and which tasks that makes.
The server's API over the store: every route and type, written before it is built.

rules.rule: The schema folders (schema/cortex, schema/ui, engines/<engine>/schema, features/<feature>/schema) are the database. Code reads and writes the tables they declare, with the columns they declare, and nothing else; no code creates, alters or drops a table, a column, an index or a constraint but the store, which does it from these files alone, and no code works out at run time what a file declares. A table, a column or a value the schema has no place for is a stop, not a workaround.

Every reference between rows is a foreign key, every value is constrained by its type and its checks, and every rule a foreign key cannot state is a rule view of its owner's rules folder (broken_<rule>, the rows breaking it), which cortex.enforce_rules turns into deferred constraint triggers: the database itself refuses any commit that breaks one, whatever code or tool wrote it. Nothing is checked by convention alone, and no code turns a check off, disables a trigger or sets session_replication_role.

What every engine shares is the cortex's; what is one engine's alone is that engine's, in its own tables in its own crate, in its own namespace engine_<engine> (engine_mysql.tables). Shared code (the model, the interface, the store, the server, the canvas) never names an engine, an engine table or an engine column; an engine never writes a cortex table's rows but through the interface, and never another engine's.

The schema grows by versions, never by rewrites. A new feature is a new owner with its own namespace, folder, versions and rules, and never changes the cortex's tables; a change to a table adds, and a rename or removal takes two versions, the data moved in the first. No version is ever edited once shipped: its checksum refuses it.

A value a person may want changed (a name, a label, a limit, a default, a link) is a row of cortex.workspace_parameters, read at run time; code holds only the key. A new value ships as a seed of a new version, inserted where its key is missing and never over a changed one.

A schema written into the store and read back is the same schema: every part, every value, every order. What the model does not describe is kept exactly as written and written back in its place. Nothing is dropped, truncated, defaulted or summarised on the way in or out.

The log (branches, turns, operations, row_changes, savepoints, versions) is appended to and never updated or deleted, but a turn's state and its verdict and a branch's newest turn; a change to the design is written in the same transaction as the operation that records it, with every row it changed, before and after.

Shared code shows what an engine declares and never assumes one: no engine's connection field, kind, option, table or column is named in it. Every test of shared code runs on every engine of the registry, and the kit checks the interface on its own made-up example engine (crates/engine/tests/example); what each engine is tested on is data.

One session, one agent, sequential: the agent that holds a task does every step itself. It never spawns, delegates to or messages another agent, subagent or session, and never asks another model to build or verify a part.

A task file lists under agent-decides the only things its agent decides: the names and the decomposition of private code inside the files it owns, the standard means of a step, the contents of its fixtures within the cases listed, its commit granularity. Everything else is written in the task file, the root, these rules, the schema folders or the merged code; a build that decides anything else is closed, and the step it departed from is named in the review.

No commit, branch, PR, file or comment carries an attribution to a coding agent or a model: no co-author line, no generated-by line, no trailer. The work is the project's: its commits are pushed under the GitHub account of whoever runs the build (decision service-accounts), reviewed and merged by the operator.

python3 tools/check.py is the one command every change passes, the same locally and in CI: no private name, XML for everything, the site as its sources render it, and, where a crate exists, formatting, lint and every test. Each objective's container proofs are its own tool (tools/cortex/all.py), run by CI beside it. Every check is a tool in the repository, never an ad-hoc command or a shell script. Nothing is done until they pass; their last lines are in the PR.

A build starts when a model is pointed at one task file, specs/tasks/<file>.xml, in any session the operator chooses (a new one, one that holds other work, or another agent's) on a checkout of the head of main updated from origin. Before it writes anything it reads, whole and in the order the root's method read gives, the files that order names, and from then on it works from them alone: nothing said earlier in the session, and nothing remembered from other work, is authority, and what the files do not say is a stop. In the database it acts only through the database's service accounts, sf_owner, sf_service and sf_reader (decision service-accounts). The task file's start element names the branch, the PR title and the read order; the agent writes its own label.
Every rule here binds every task, whether or not a gate of the task names it.

helping.do: Report what you understood first, in your own words, and ask your human what they want to do.

Start from an issue (https://github.com/k8nstantin/schema-forge/issues, good first issue for a start) or a question in Discussions (https://github.com/k8nstantin/schema-forge/discussions). Larger work is agreed with the maintainer before code, often as a task file.
Never change specs/, an owner's folder (schema/, engines/*/schema, features/), owner.toml or postgres/manifest.toml: they change only in a design session with the maintainer.
One issue, one branch, one pull request; python3 tools/check.py and the objective's own tools (tools/cortex/all.py) pass before you push (they need Docker).
No attribution of any kind in commits or pull requests: your human is the author, and answers for every line.
Ask your human before you open an issue, push, comment or open a pull request: those speak for them.
